claims.text: Sustained creep loading causes progressive plastic deformation in nanoscale FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers.
Progressive plastic deformation in these multilayers is predominantly governed by interface-mediated dislocation accumulation.
Severe lattice distortion at FCC/BCC interfaces impedes conventional dislocation glide.
Pronounced short-range order at FCC/BCC interfaces impedes conventional dislocation glide.
Interfacial barriers produced by lattice distortion and short-range order lead to dislocation pile-ups.
Dislocation pile-ups eventually trigger localized interface slip or dislocation climb.
The as-deposited multilayers have a low initial dislocation density.
The as-deposited multilayers possess inherent lattice distortion and short-range order.
Controlled elevated-temperature creep activates thermally assisted irreversible dislocation motion while preserving the multilayer architecture.
Nanoscale FCC/BCC interfaces enhance dislocation accumulation because of their lattice distortion and chemical complexity.
Dislocations generated within individual layers are impeded at heterogeneous FCC/BCC interfaces during sustained loading.
The stress produced by accumulated dislocations can overcome the interfacial barrier.
Overcoming the interfacial barrier triggers interface slip, dislocation climb, or cross-boundary dislocation transfer.
The localized interfacial events produce progressive, strain-localized deformation.
Greater interfacial lattice distortion and short-range order delay the onset of plastic deformation.
After the delayed onset, greater interfacial lattice distortion and short-range order accelerate and localize strain accumulation.
Greater interfacial lattice distortion and short-range order increase local dislocation density and produce observable interface-structure changes relative to the starting baseline.
The proposed mechanism is limited to nanoscale multilayers under creep conditions that avoid catastrophic failure, excessive intermixing, and phase transformation.
The role of dislocation accumulation is supported.
High-order, highly distorted interfaces should show earlier or more pronounced plastic deformation than interfaces with minimized ordering and distortion.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome says stronger lattice distortion and short-range order delay the onset of plastic deformation, whereas the falsification rule expects the same samples to display earlier or more pronounced plastic deformation. The timing criterion therefore conflicts with the stated prediction.
